claims.claim: ACC-4 may act as an inhibitory autoreceptor on cholinergic neurons.
claims.source: raising the intriguing possibility that ACC-4 may act as an inhibitory autoreceptor on cholinergic neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observation that some acc-4 expressing neurons are not innervated by other cholinergic neurons.

claims.claim: In the context of gene expression networks, negative autoregulation can confer a number of useful functions, including speed-up of circuit responses and noise reduction.
claims.source: In the context of gene expression networks, negative autoregulation can confer a number of useful functions, including speed-up of circuit responses and noise reduction (Hart and Alon, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hart and Alon, 2013.

claims.claim: The C. elegans male contains 91 sex-specific neurons, defining 24 classes, most of them located in the tail.
claims.source: The C. elegans male contains 91 sex-specific neurons, defining 24 classes, most of them located in the tail.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the anatomy of the male nervous system.

claims.claim: 16 out of 24 male-specific neuron classes are cholinergic.
claims.source: We find that 16 out of these 24 classes are cholinergic (Figure 5A, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Table 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5A, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Table 5.

claims.claim: The CEM sensory neurons are the only male-specific head neurons and are cholinergic.
claims.source: These cholinergic neurons include the only male-specific head neurons (the CEM sensory neurons)
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of neurotransmitter identity in male-specific neurons.

claims.claim: The CA neurons are an additional, male-specific class of motor neurons in the ventral nerve cord.
claims.source: and an additional, male-specific class of motor neurons in the ventral nerve cord, the CA neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of neurotransmitter identity in male-specific neurons.

claims.claim: ACh is the most broadly used neurotransmitter in the male nervous system.
claims.source: The three key themes observed in the hermaphrodite nervous system also apply to the male-specific neurons: (1) ACh is the most broadly used neurotransmitter in the male nervous system
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of neurotransmitter identity in male-specific neurons.

claims.claim: ACh is used in sensory, inter- and motor neurons of the male-specific nervous system.
claims.source: (2) ACh is used in sensory, inter- and motor neurons of the male-specific nervous system
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of neurotransmitter identity in male-specific neurons.

claims.claim: The male-specific sensory neurons that are cholinergic are all in close proximity to the motor circuitry.
claims.source: (3) the male-specific sensory neurons that are cholinergic are all in close proximity to the motor circuitry: most of them directly innervate muscle (i.e. are sensory/motor neurons; PCB, PCC, SPC; several ray neurons) while all others (HOB, SPV) innervate motor neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of the connectome.

claims.claim: The PVV neurons and the R6A neurons express unc-17/VAChT and eat-4/VGLUT.
claims.source: Like in the pharyngeal nervous system, we found neurons labeled by two conventional fast transmitters markers– the PVV neurons and the R6A neurons express unc-17/VAChT and eat-4/VGLUT (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' observations of reporter gene expression.

claims.claim: ACh/Glu cotransmission has been observed in some central synapses in the vertebrate central nervous system.
claims.source: ACh/Glu cotransmission has been observed in some central synapses in the vertebrate central nervous system (Nishimaru et al., 2005; Ren et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nishimaru et al., 2005 and Ren et al., 2011.

claims.claim: The male-specific CEM neurons are generated in the embryo in both sexes, but are removed specifically in the hermaphrodite through programmed cell death.
claims.source: The two pairs of CEM neurons are generated in the embryo in both sexes, but are removed specifically in the hermaphrodite through programmed cell death (Sulston et al., 1983).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sulston et al., 1983.

claims.claim: The CEM neurons only start expressing cholinergic identity features at the L4 larval stage.
claims.source: We examined the onset of cholinergic differentiation of these neurons in males and found that they only start expressing cholinergic identity features at the L4 larval stage (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The HSN and VC neurons are hermaphrodite-specific cholinergic neurons.
claims.source: The same applies to the two classes of hermaphrodite-specific cholinergic neurons, the HSN and VC neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of neurotransmitter identity.

claims.claim: HSN is born embryonically, and VCs are born in the first larval stage, yet onset of cholinergic pathway genes is only observed in late L4 larval stages.
claims.source: HSN is born embryonically, and VCs are born in the first larval stage, yet onset of cholinergic pathway genes is only observed in late L4 larval stages (Figure 5B–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5B-C.

claims.claim: The onset of cholinergic marker expression in the VC neurons is observed in late L4 stage animals, contrasting the late L1 onset in the VA, VB and AS-type neurons.
claims.source: In these neurons, the onset of cholinergic marker expression is observed already in late L1 stage animals, contrasting the late L4 onset in the VC neurons (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The AIM neuron pair expresses cholinergic markers only in males, but not hermaphrodites.
claims.source: We were therefore surprised to note a pair of neurons, located next to the cholinergic AIY interneurons in the ventral head ganglion that expressed cholinergic markers only in males, but not hermaphrodites (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: In hermaphrodites, the AIM neurons are glutamatergic, expressing the vesicular glutamate transporter eat-4/VGLUT.
claims.source: In hermaphrodites, the AIM neurons are glutamatergic, expressing the vesicular glutamate transporter eat-4/VGLUT (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: In males, the AIM neurons also initially express eat-4/VGLUT, but only until the L3 stage.
claims.source: In males, the AIM neurons also initially express eat-4/VGLUT, but only until the L3 stage.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' observations of reporter gene expression.

claims.claim: During the L4 stage in males, eat-4/VGLUT expression becomes downregulated and unc-17/VAChT and cho-1/ChT expression becomes induced in AIM neurons.
claims.source: During the L4 stage eat-4/VGLUT expression becomes downregulated and unc-17/VAChT and cho-1/ChT expression becomes induced (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Masculinization of the AIM neurons in otherwise hermaphroditic animals results in downregulation of eat-4/VGLUT and upregulation of cho-1 expression.
claims.source: We found that masculinization of the AIM neurons ('eat-4prom11::fem-3') in otherwise hermaphroditic animals results in downregulation of eat-4/VGLUT and upregulation of cho-1 expression (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Feminization of AIM in male animals results in sustained eat-4 expression and no induction of cho-1 expression.
claims.source: Conversely, feminization of AIM in male animals results in sustained eat-4 expression and no induction of cho-1 expression (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The neurotransmitter switch in AIM neurons is programmed cell autonomously.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that the neurotransmitter switch is programmed cell autonomously.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' experimental results showing that cell-specific manipulation of sex determination genes affects neurotransmitter identity.

claims.claim: The POU homeobox gene unc-86 controls the cholinergic identity of three cholinergic sensory neurons (IL2, URA, URB).
claims.source: Specifically, we have reported that the POU homeobox gene unc-86 controls the cholinergic identity of three cholinergic sensory neurons (IL2, URA, URB) (Zhang et al., 2014)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The LIM homeobox gene ttx-3 controls the cholinergic identity of two cholinergic interneurons (AIY, AIA).
claims.source: that the LIM homeobox gene ttx-3 controls the cholinergic identity of two cholinergic interneurons (AIY, AIA) (Altun-Gultekin et al., 2001)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Altun-Gultekin et al., 2001.

claims.claim: The COE (Collier/Olf/EBF)-type Zn-finger factor unc-3 controls cholinergic identity of most motor neuron classes in the VNC as well as the SAB head motor neurons.
claims.source: and that the COE (Collier/Olf/EBF)-type Zn-finger factor unc-3 controls cholinergic identity of most motor neuron classes in the VNC as well as the SAB head motor neurons (Kratsios et al., 2011, 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kratsios et al., 2011 and 2015.

claims.claim: A total of 7 regulators control the identity of 20 of the 52 cholinergic neuron types.
claims.source: Our analysis resulted in the identification of a total of 7 regulators that control the identity of 20 of the 52 cholinergic neuron types (Table 6; Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Table 6 and Figure 6.

claims.claim: There is a striking preponderance of homeodomain containing proteins in the transcription factors that regulate cholinergic identity.
claims.source: In line with a similar observation that we made upon analysis of glutamatergic neuron identity control (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013), we observed a striking preponderance of homeodomain containing proteins in the transcription factors that we newly identified as cholinergic identity regulators.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of the transcription factors identified and cites Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The three LIM homeobox genes lim-4, lin-11 and ceh-14 control cholinergic identity of six distinct cholinergic neuron types.
claims.source: Specifically, we found that the three LIM homeobox genes lim-4, lin-11 and ceh-14 control cholinergic identity of six distinct cholinergic neuron types, including sensory neurons (lim-4 in AWB), interneurons (lin-11 in PVP; ceh-14 in AIM, PVC) and motor neurons (ceh-14 in PVN, lim-4 in SMB; Table 6; Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Table 6 and Figure 6.

claims.claim: lim-7, the C. elegans homolog of vertebrate Islet, is not required to specify cholinergic identity in C. elegans.
claims.source: However, we find that lim-7, the C. elegans homolog of vertebrate Islet, which specifies cholinergic identity in the spinal cord and forebrain in mice (Cho et al., 2014), is not required to specify cholinergic identity in C. elegans (as assessed by normal cho-1 expression throughout the nervous system in lim-7 null mutants; data not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' experimental observations and cites Cho et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The Pitx-type homeobox gene unc-30 controls cholinergic identity of the PVP interneurons (in conjunction with lin-11).
claims.source: Moreover, we found that the Pitx-type homeobox gene unc-30 controls cholinergic identity of the PVP interneurons (in conjunction with lin-11)
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' experimental observations.

claims.claim: The POU homeobox gene unc-86 controls cholinergic identity of the URX, RIH and male-specific CEM neurons.
claims.source: and that the POU homeobox gene unc-86 controls cholinergic identity of the URX, RIH and male-specific CEM neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' experimental observations.

claims.claim: unc-86, in conjunction with ceh-14, is required for the AIM neurons to adopt their cholinergic identity in males.
claims.source: unc-86, in conjunction with ceh-14, is also required for the AIM neurons to adopt their cholinergic identity in males
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' experimental observations.

claims.claim: unc-86 and ceh-14 also control glutamatergic identity of the AIM neurons in hermaphrodites (and males till the third larval stage).
claims.source: both factors also control glutamatergic identity of the AIM neurons in hermaphrodites (and males till the third larval stage; Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6.

claims.claim: All of the transcription factors that control cholinergic identity are continuously expressed throughout the life of these neurons.
claims.source: All of the above-mentioned transcription factors are continuously expressed throughout the life of these neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that these factors not only initiate but also maintain cholinergic identity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: unc-42, a Prox-type homeobox gene, is a regulator of cholinergic gene expression in RMD motor neurons.
claims.source: From a EMS-induced genetic mutant screen that we conducted for regulators of RMD neuron identity (see Materials and methods), we uncovered unc-42, a Prox-type homeobox gene as a regulator of cholinergic gene expression in RMD motor neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' genetic screen.

claims.claim: unc-42 affects cholinergic identity of four additional, distinct types of cholinergic head neurons, most of them motor neurons.
claims.source: We also found that unc-42 affects cholinergic identity of four additional, distinct types of cholinergic head neurons, most of them motor neurons (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6.

claims.claim: unc-42 is continuously expressed in all the postmitotic neuron types it regulates.
claims.source: unc-42 is continuously expressed in all these postmitotic neuron types (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: unc-3 regulates expression of the cholinergic identity genes cho-1 and unc-17 in all command interneurons.
claims.source: In addition to the previously reported impact of unc-3 on cholinergic ventral cord motor neuron identity (SAB-, A-, B-, AS-type MNs), we found that unc-3 regulates expression of the cholinergic identity genes cho-1 and unc-17 in all command interneurons (Figure 7, Table 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7 and Table 6.

claims.claim: The PDA, PDB, PVN and DVA tail neurons require unc-3 for their normal expression of cholinergic identity genes.
claims.source: Moreover, the PDA, PDB, PVN and DVA tail neurons also require unc-3 for their normal expression of cholinergic identity genes (Figure 7, Table 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7 and Table 6.

claims.claim: unc-3 is expressed in all the cholinergic neuron types it regulates, including the command interneurons.
claims.source: Using a fosmid reporter and a gfp reporter inserted into the unc-3 locus through CRISPR-Cas9, we confirmed expression of unc-3 in all these cholinergic neuron types, including the command interneurons (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Most of the transcriptional regulators that control cholinergic identity also control other identity features.
claims.source: Most of the transcriptional regulators that we defined here control not only cholinergic identity in the respective neuron classes, but also control other identity features.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of the effects of transcription factor mutations.

claims.claim: Loss of unc-3 affects multiple aspects of PDA motor neuron identity (expression of the exp-1 ligand gated ion channel, ace-3/4 cholinesterase, cog-1 homeobox gene).
claims.source: For example, we find that loss of unc-3 affects multiple aspects of PDA motor neuron identity (expression of the exp-1 ligand gated ion channel, ace-3/4 cholinesterase, cog-1 homeobox gene)
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' experimental observations.

claims.claim: Loss of unc-42 affects metabotropic glutamate receptor (mgl-1) expression in the RMD neurons.
claims.source: and loss of unc-42 affects metabotropic glutamate receptor (mgl-1) expression in the RMD neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' experimental observations.

claims.claim: Loss of ceh-14 affects neuropeptide (flp-10) expression, as well as the serotonergic co-transmitter identity of the AIM neurons and it affects expression of the ionotropic glutamate receptors nmr-1 and glr-1 in the PVC command interneuron.
claims.source: Apart from affecting cholinergic identity, loss of ceh-14 affects neuropeptide (flp-10) expression, as well as the serotonergic co-transmitter identity of the AIM neurons and it affects expression of the ionotropic glutamate receptors nmr-1 and glr-1 in the PVC command interneuron (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8.

claims.claim: lin-11 and unc-30 control many terminal identity features of the PVP.
claims.source: In addition, lin-11 and unc-30 were previously found to control many terminal identity features of the PVP (Hutter, 2003) and these two factors also control cholinergic identity of PVP (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hutter, 2003 and data presented in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: lim-4 controls cholinergic identity of the AWB neurons but also several other identity features.
claims.source: Similarly, lim-4 controls cholinergic identity of the AWB neurons but also several other identity features (Alqadah et al., 2015; Sagasti et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alqadah et al., 2015 and Sagasti et al., 1999.

claims.claim: The serotonergic identity of the hermaphrodite specific motor neurons HSN is controlled by the unc-86 POU homeobox gene.
claims.source: The serotonergic identity of the hermaphrodite specific motor neurons HSN is controlled by the unc-86 POU homeobox gene (Sze et al., 2002)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sze et al., 2002.

claims.claim: unc-86 does not affect unc-17/VAChT expression in HSN.
claims.source: but unc-86 does not affect unc-17/VAChT expression in HSN (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' experimental observations.

claims.claim: In all motor neurons in which unc-3 is expressed (SAB head motor neurons, A- B- and AS-type VNC MNs), unc-3 controls neurotransmitter identity and a multitude of other terminal molecular markers.
claims.source: We had previously shown that in all motor neurons in which unc-3 is expressed (SAB head motor neurons, A- B- and AS-type VNC MNs), unc-3 not only controls neurotransmitter identity, but also a multitude of other terminal molecular markers (Kratsios et al., 2015, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kratsios et al., 2015 and 2011.

claims.claim: The activity of unc-3 in the AVA, AVB, AVD, AVE and PVC command interneurons and DVA interneuron appears to be restricted to select subfeatures of these neurons.
claims.source: In contrast, the activity of unc-3 in the AVA, AVB, AVD, AVE and PVC command interneurons and DVA interneuron appears to be restricted to select subfeatures of these neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of the effects of unc-3 mutations.

claims.claim: Not a single identity marker besides the cholinergic reporter genes is affected in the command interneurons and DVA interneuron in worms lacking unc-3.
claims.source: We arrived at this conclusion by analyzing the expression of more than ten additional identity markers of these unc-3-expressing neurons (including glutamate receptors, neuropeptides and ion channels). Not a single one besides the cholinergic reporter genes is affected in the worms lacking unc-3 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Table 7).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Table 7.

claims.claim: Within the command interneurons AVA, AVD and AVE, three transcription factors, unc-42 (homeobox), fax-1 (nuclear hormone receptor) and cfi-1 (ARID-type), control subsets of unc-3-independent terminal identity markers.
claims.source: Within a subset of these neurons, namely the command interneurons AVA, AVD and AVE, three transcription factors, unc-42 (homeobox), fax-1 (nuclear hormone receptor) and cfi-1 (ARID-type), have been shown to control subsets of these unc-3-independent terminal identity markers (Table 8).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Table 8.

claims.claim: unc-3 is expressed and required for the adoption of cholinergic identity in all neurons in the ventral nerve cord motor circuit.
claims.source: Strikingly, unc-3 is expressed and required for the adoption of cholinergic identity in all neurons in this circuit (schematized in Figure 9A; data in Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 9A and Figure 7B.

claims.claim: unc-3 is a circuit-associated transcription factor that is selectively associated with the ventral nerve cord motor circuit.
claims.source: unc-3 is therefore a circuit-associated transcription factor that is selectively associated with this circuit (unc-3 is expressed only in a few neurons outside this circuit) and that defines a critical feature of the circuit, namely the ability of neurons in the circuit to communicate among each other.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of unc-3 expression and function.

claims.claim: In unc-3 mutants, UNC-7::GFP puncta, which visualize electrical synapses, are severely reduced.
claims.source: UNC-7::GFP puncta, visualized with a translational reporter are severely reduced in unc-3 mutants (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Expression of a transcriptional, fosmid-based unc-7 reporter is unaffected in unc-3 mutants.
claims.source: Expression of a transcriptional, fosmid-based unc-7 reporter is unaffected in unc-3 mutants (data not shown)
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' experimental observations.

claims.claim: unc-3 affects electrical synapse formation at a step independent of regulation of innexin expression.
claims.source: leading us to conclude that unc-3 affects electrical synapse formation at a step independent of regulation of innexin expression.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that transcriptional unc-7 expression is unaffected but UNC-7::GFP puncta are reduced.

claims.claim: In unc-3 null mutants, AVA receives less chemical synaptic input from within the motor circuit and it makes less chemical synapses onto other motor neurons and onto other command interneurons.
claims.source: In unc-3 null mutants, we found connectivity defects on all levels: AVA receives less chemical synaptic input from within the motor circuit (i.e. from other command interneurons) and it makes less chemical synapses onto other motor neurons and onto other command interneurons (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: There is an overall disorganization of the placement of axonal processes in the VNC of unc-3 mutants.
claims.source: There is also an overall disorganization of the placement of axonal processes in the VNC of unc-3 mutants (data not shown)
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' experimental observations.

claims.claim: In unc-3 mutants, AVA still neighbors the command interneurons that it normally connects to, indicating that the connectivity defects are not a secondary consequence of placement defects.
claims.source: however, AVA still neighbors the command interneurons that it normally connects to, indicating that the connectivity defects are not a secondary consequence of placement defects.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that AVA is still adjacent to its normal synaptic partners despite connectivity defects.

claims.claim: Non-cholinergic synaptic inputs from sensory neurons into the motor circuit appear not to be affected by unc-3.
claims.source: Non-cholinergic synaptic inputs from sensory neurons into the motor circuit appear not to be affected by unc-3.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' experimental observations.

claims.claim: The synaptic connection of the glutamatergic PHB neuron to the AVA interneuron is unaffected in unc-3 mutants.
claims.source: We arrived at this conclusion by examining the synaptic connections of the glutamatergic PHB neuron to the AVA interneuron, normally made in the pre-anal ganglion (White et al., 1986). This synaptic connection can be visualized using a GFP reconstitution system ('GRASP'; (Park et al., 2011). We find these synaptic GFP signals to be unaffected in unc-3 mutants (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' experimental observations using GRASP and cites White et al., 1986 and Park et al., 2011.

claims.claim: The pan-circuit control of cholinergic neurotransmitter identity by unc-3 is mediated via a single UNC-3 binding site ('COE motif') controlling neurotransmitter pathway genes.
claims.source: Remarkably, the pan-circuit control of cholinergic neurotransmitter identity by unc-3 is mediated via a single UNC-3 binding site ('COE motif') controlling neurotransmitter pathway genes.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' experimental observations.

claims.claim: Deletion of the COE motif in the context of the cho-1/ChT fosmid-based reporter eliminates expression not only in the ventral nerve cord motor neurons, but also in all other unc-3 dependent cholinergic neurons.
claims.source: Its deletion in the context of the cho-1/ChT fosmid-based reporter eliminates expression not only in the ventral nerve cord motor neurons, but also in all other unc-3 dependent cholinergic neurons, not just within the motor neuron circuit, but also outside the circuit (Figure 10A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 10A-C.

claims.claim: A 280 bp region from the cho-1 and a 250 bp region from the unc-17 locus that contain the COE motif are not sufficient to drive expression in all unc-3-dependent inter- and motor neurons of the motor circuit, but only drives expression in motor neurons.
claims.source: On the other hand, a 280 bp region from the cho-1 and a 250 bp region from the unc-17 locus that contain the COE motif are not sufficient to drive expression in all unc-3-dependent inter- and motor neurons of the motor circuit, but only drives expression in motor neurons (Figure 10D, E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 10D and E.

claims.claim: unc-3 may cooperate with distinct cofactors in distinct neuron types.
claims.source: This finding suggests that unc-3 may cooperate with distinct cofactors in distinct neuron types.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that a short COE motif-containing fragment is not sufficient to drive expression in all unc-3-dependent neurons.

claims.claim: unc-3 activity is required not only for the expression of proper neurotransmitter identity, but also for synaptic connectivity throughout the VNC motor neuron circuit.
claims.source: Taken together, unc-3 activity is required not only for the expression of proper neurotransmitter identity, but also for synaptic connectivity throughout the VNC motor neuron circuit, not just in motor neurons but also in command interneurons.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement based on the authors' experimental observations.

claims.claim: unc-3 is not required to control the expression of other identity features of command interneurons, such as the many types of distinct glutamate receptors expressed by the command interneurons.
claims.source: However, as mentioned above, unc-3 is not required to control the expression of other identity features of command interneurons, such as the many types of distinct glutamate receptors expressed by the command interneurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The homeobox gene unc-42 is frequently employed in the context of the 'regulated mutual' 3-neuron network motif.
claims.source: On a micro-circuit level, we note that the homeobox gene unc-42 is, like unc-3, also frequently employed in the context of the 'regulated mutual' 3-neuron network motif described above.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of network motifs and unc-42 function.

claims.claim: unc-42 specifies the cholinergic identity of the cross-connected head motor neurons (RMDs, SMDs) and the RIV interneuron that innervates these cross-connected neurons.
claims.source: In the case of the cross-connected head motor neurons (RMDs, SMDs) and the RIV interneuron that innervates these cross-connected neurons, unc-42 specifies the cholinergic identity of all of these neurons (and other signaling input to these neurons, exemplified by the above-mentioned regulation of the metabotropic Glu receptor mgl-1 by unc-42).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' experimental observations.

claims.claim: In the cross-connected command interneurons, unc-42 does not affect their cholinergic identity, but it does affect the expression of multiple ionotropic Glu receptors (GluRs) expressed in the command interneurons.
claims.source: In the cross-connected command interneurons, unc-42 does not affect their cholinergic identity, but it does affect the expression of multiple ionotropic Glu receptors (GluRs) expressed in the command interneurons (Brockie et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brockie et al., 2001.

claims.claim: The glutamatergic identity of the ASH neurons is controlled by unc-42.
claims.source: We previously found that the glutamatergic identity of the ASH neurons is controlled by unc-42 (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013.

claims.claim: unc-42 controls and apparently coordinates the expression of presynaptic neurotransmitter identity and postsynaptic receptor expression in a repulsive reflex circuit.
claims.source: unc-42 therefore controls and apparently coordinates the expression of presynaptic neurotransmitter identity and postsynaptic receptor expression in a repulsive reflex circuit (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 9B and is an inference based on the authors' observations.

claims.claim: Mutually connected, unc-42-dependent head motor neurons are coupled by electrical synapses.
claims.source: Mutually connected, unc-42-dependent head motor neurons are coupled by electrical synapses (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: The glutamatergic identity of the AIB interneurons is controlled by unc-42.
claims.source: This connection is made by the glutamatergic AIB interneurons; strikingly, their glutamatergic identity is also controlled by unc-42 (E.S. and O.H., unpubl. data).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on unpublished data from the authors.

claims.claim: A network of interconnected neurons in the head of the worm that employ distinct neurotransmitter systems all require unc-42, either for the acquisition of their neurotransmitter identity or for the ability to receive neurotransmitter signals.
claims.source: Taken together, a network of interconnected neurons in the head of the worm that employ distinct neurotransmitter systems all require unc-42, either for the acquisition of their neurotransmitter identity or for the ability to receive neurotransmitter signals (unc-42-dependent GluR expression in command interneurons).
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement based on the authors' experimental observations.

results.result: Acetylcholine (ACh) is the most broadly used neurotransmitter in C. elegans, expressed in 52 of 118 neuron classes (159 of 302 neurons) in hermaphrodites, and 85% of all neuron classes are innervated by cholinergic neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7, C8, C9, C10, and C11 collectively demonstrate that ACh is the predominant neurotransmitter system. The data showing 52/118 neuron classes express unc-17/VAChT (C8), that 85% of neurons receive cholinergic input (C9), and that all but one neuron class (CAN) are connected to the cholinergic system (C10, C11) provide strong, converging evidence from fosmid reporter expression and connectome analysis.

results.result: The hermaphrodite nervous system contains 6 GABAergic neuron classes (26 neurons), 38 glutamatergic classes (78 neurons), and 13 aminergic classes (26 neurons).
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, and C4 are supported by citations to prior published work (McIntire et al., 1993; Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013; Chase and Koelle, 2007). These claims provide context for comparing ACh usage to other neurotransmitter systems and are well-established in the literature.

results.result: Previous antibody staining methods for VAChT and ChAT could only unambiguously assign cholinergic identity to about one dozen neuron classes due to synaptic localization of these proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C6 accurately describe limitations of prior work (Alfonso et al., 1993; Duerr et al., 2008). The authors' interpretation that synaptic localization limited cell identification is consistent with the cited literature and provides justification for their fosmid-based approach.

results.result: The choline transporter cho-1/ChT expression extensively correlates with unc-17/VAChT expression, with all cho-1-expressing neurons also expressing unc-17, but 11 of 52 unc-17(+) classes do not express cho-1.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C13, and C14 are supported by fosmid reporter expression data presented in Figure 1 and Table 1. The asymmetric overlap pattern (all cho-1+ are unc-17+, but not vice versa) is clearly documented and provides insight into cholinergic pathway gene regulation.

results.result: Acetylcholinesterase (ace) gene expression does not correlate with unc-17 expression; only one-third of cholinergic neurons express ace genes, and ace expression is also observed in body wall muscle and non-cholinergic neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C15, C16, and C17 are supported by data in Table 1 and Figure 1H, consistent with prior work (Combes et al., 2003). The lack of correlation between AChE and cholinergic identity is expected given that secreted AChE acts in the synaptic cleft and need not be synthesized in the same cells that release ACh.

results.result: There are no overlaps in usage of the main neurotransmitter systems (glutamate, GABA, ACh) in the core nervous system of the hermaphrodite, except for the pharyngeal M5 neuron which expresses both cholinergic and glutamatergic markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C18 and C19 are supported by the authors' systematic analysis of neurotransmitter marker expression (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2). The single exception (M5) is clearly documented, and the general lack of overlap is consistent with the mutually exclusive expression patterns observed.

results.result: Some neurons exhibit co-transmission of ACh with aminergic neurotransmitters: ADF, HSN, RIH, and VC4/5 are both cholinergic and serotonergic, with VC4/5 notably lacking cho-1 expression despite expressing unc-17.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C23 are supported by citations to prior work (Duerr et al., 2001; Sze et al., 2000; Duerr et al., 1999) and the authors' own observations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 5C). The correlation between serotonergic identity and absence of cho-1 in VC4/5 is an interesting observation that suggests differential regulation of cholinergic pathway genes.

results.result: ACh is used by sensory neurons, interneurons, and motor neurons, with motor neurons showing a preference for ACh (17/24 classes), while sensory neurons are predominantly glutamatergic (22/38) but include an appreciable number of cholinergic classes (9/38).
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28 are supported by data in Figure 2A and Table 2. The quantitative breakdown by neuron type provides important functional context for understanding ACh usage patterns across different neuronal classes.

results.result: Most cholinergic sensory neurons have shallow processing depth (close to motor output), with some directly synapsing onto muscle or motor neurons, and URX/AWB forming the only all-cholinergic multi-neuron pathways from sensory to motor neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 are supported by connectome analysis presented in Figure 2B. The observation that cholinergic sensory neurons are positioned close to motor output, in contrast to glutamatergic sensory neurons, is a novel finding that suggests functional specialization of cholinergic sensory pathways.

results.result: ACh is the most broadly used neurotransmitter of interneurons (19 classes vs. 11 glutamatergic), while GABA is sparsely used by interneurons (1 class), though both ACh and Glu can act as inhibitory neurotransmitters via chloride channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 are supported by data in Figure 2A and Table 1, with C36 citing McIntire et al., 1993. Claim C37 is based on established knowledge about ACh- and Glu-gated chloride channels and is elaborated later in the manuscript with expression data for acc genes.

results.result: The command interneurons (AVA, AVB, AVD, AVE, PVC) are cholinergic, as confirmed by expression of unc-17 and cho-1 fosmid reporters and co-expression with glutamate receptor markers (glr-1, nmr-1) or ACh receptor markers (sra-11, acr-15).
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C41 are supported by fosmid reporter expression data and co-staining experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The identification of command interneurons as cholinergic is a novel finding of major importance, as these neurons are central integrators of information flow, as established by prior work (Chalfie et al., 1985; Von Stetina et al., 2006).

results.result: Cholinergic neurotransmitter identity does not correlate with neuronal position (except for VNC motor neurons) or developmental lineage history.
results.evaluation: Claims C42 and C43 are supported by data in Figure 2C and 2D. The lack of spatial or lineage clustering of cholinergic neurons (with the noted exception) suggests that cholinergic identity is specified by cell-type-specific transcriptional programs rather than by position or lineage.

results.result: With the complete cholinergic map, neurotransmitter identity can now be assigned to ~90% of all neuron classes (102/118), with about half of the remaining 'orphan' neurons showing a paucity of synaptic vesicles, suggesting they may signal via electrical synapses or neuropeptides.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46 are supported by data in Table 2 and EM analysis from White et al., 1986. The high percentage of neurons with assigned neurotransmitter identity represents a major advance. Claim C46 is speculative but reasonable given the EM observations of vesicle paucity.

results.result: The ventral nerve cord motor circuit is predominantly cholinergic, with all motor neurons (SAB, DA, DB, VA, VB, AS) and all innervating command interneurons (AVA, AVB, AVE, AVD, PVC, DVA) using ACh, forming a 'rich club' of interconnected neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 are supported by data in Figure 3B and citation to Towlson et al., 2013. The finding that an entire functional circuit uses a single neurotransmitter system is striking and suggests coordinated regulation of circuit identity.

results.result: Genetic silencing of the nervous system via snb-1/synaptobrevin elimination does not affect cholinergic identity marker expression in arrested L1 larvae.
results.evaluation: Claim C51 is based on the authors' experimental observations (data not shown). While the data are not presented, this control experiment addresses whether neural activity is required for cholinergic identity expression, which is relevant to understanding the developmental program.

results.result: Compared to glutamate, ACh is enriched but not exclusively located at lower levels of information processing (closer to motor output).
results.evaluation: Claim C52 is supported by processing depth analysis in Figure 3C and 3D. This finding is consistent with the observation that cholinergic sensory neurons have shallow processing depth and that motor neurons preferentially use ACh.

results.result: Five 3-neuron and fourteen 4-neuron motifs are significantly enriched in the C. elegans connectome, with ACh enriched at specific positions in 11 of 19 motifs, showing a trend of ACh at downstream positions and Glu at upstream positions.
results.evaluation: Claims C53, C55, and C56 are supported by network motif analysis in Figure 3E using methods from Milo et al., 2002. The positional enrichment of neurotransmitters within motifs provides insight into how neurotransmitter identity relates to circuit architecture and information flow.

results.result: The 'regulated mutual motif' (224 occurrences) is significantly enriched for cholinergic neurons in positions 2 and 3 and glutamatergic neurons in position 1, with two main types: (1) glutamatergic sensory neurons innervating reciprocally connected cholinergic command interneurons controlling opposite movement directions, and (2) sensory neurons innervating reciprocally connected cholinergic head motor neurons (SMD/RMD).
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C65 are supported by network motif analysis and connectome data presented in Table 4 and Figure 3E, citing Milo et al., 2004. The detailed characterization of neurotransmitter usage within this specific motif type reveals organizational principles of circuit architecture.

results.result: The C. elegans genome encodes at least four ACh-gated anion channels (acc-1 through acc-4), with acc-1 and acc-2 electrophysiologically validated as inhibitory receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are supported by citations to Hobert, 2013 and Putrenko et al., 2005. These claims provide essential background for interpreting the expression patterns of acc genes examined in this study.

results.result: acc-3 shows no appreciable expression, while acc-1 and acc-2 show restricted, non-overlapping expression in subsets of cholinergic and glutamatergic neurons, with acc-1 in VNC neurons, head motor neurons, and command interneurons, and acc-2 in distinct glutamatergic (RIA, RIG, PHA, AIZ) and cholinergic (URX, RIH) neurons plus male-specific MCM neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 are supported by fosmid reporter expression data in Figure 4. The restricted expression patterns of acc-1 and acc-2 suggest specific roles in inhibitory cholinergic signaling in particular circuits.

results.result: The acc-4 fosmid reporter is expressed almost exclusively in almost all 52 classes of cholinergic neurons (except ASJ and RIB), with the only non-cholinergic expression in AVF neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are supported by fosmid reporter expression data in Figure 4 showing extensive co-expression of acc-4 with cho-1. The nearly complete overlap with cholinergic neurons is striking and suggests a broad role for acc-4 in cholinergic signaling.

results.result: If acc-4 operates as an inhibitory receptor, most cholinergic neurons can be silenced by presynaptically released ACh, consistent with more than half of cholinergic neurons being innervated by other cholinergic neurons, including cross-inhibitory command interneurons that can function as toggle switches.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 combine expression data (C79, supported by connectome analysis) with functional speculation (C78, C81). While the expression pattern and connectivity are well-documented, the functional role of acc-4 as an inhibitory receptor remains conditional ('if acc-4 indeed is able to operate as inhibitory receptor'). Electrophysiological validation of acc-4 function is needed. The toggle switch model (C81) is based on general knowledge but requires experimental validation in this specific context.

results.result: Many cholinergic neurons also express excitatory ACh-gated ion channels (acr genes), and a substantial number of acc-4-expressing cholinergic neurons are not innervated by other cholinergic neurons, raising the possibility that ACC-4 may act as an inhibitory autoreceptor, which could provide circuit speed-up and noise reduction.
results.evaluation: Claim C82 is supported by WormBase data. Claim C83 is supported by connectome analysis. However, claims C84 and C85 are speculative. The autoreceptor hypothesis is intriguing but requires experimental validation. The functional benefits cited in C85 (Hart and Alon, 2013) are from gene regulatory networks, not synaptic signaling, so the analogy may not hold.

results.result: The C. elegans male contains 91 sex-specific neurons (24 classes), with 16 classes being cholinergic, including the CEM head sensory neurons and CA ventral nerve cord motor neurons, showing the same themes as hermaphrodites: ACh is the most broadly used neurotransmitter, used in sensory/inter/motor neurons, with cholinergic sensory neurons close to motor circuitry.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C92 are supported by data in Figure 5A, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Table 5. The extension of the cholinergic map to male-specific neurons demonstrates that the organizational principles observed in hermaphrodites also apply to the male nervous system.

results.result: The male-specific PVV and R6A neurons express both unc-17/VAChT and eat-4/VGLUT, similar to the pharyngeal M5 neuron, representing potential ACh/Glu co-transmission as observed in vertebrate CNS.
results.evaluation: Claim C93 is based on the authors' observations (data not shown). Claim C94 provides vertebrate precedent (Nishimaru et al., 2005; Ren et al., 2011). While the data are not shown, the observation is consistent with the M5 finding and vertebrate examples.

results.result: Sex-specific cholinergic neurons (male CEM, hermaphrodite HSN and VC) are generated early in development but only express cholinergic identity features at the L4 larval stage during sexual maturation, contrasting with other motor neurons (VA, VB, AS) that express cholinergic markers in late L1.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C99 are supported by developmental time course data in Figure 5A-C and citation to Sulston et al., 1983. The late onset of cholinergic identity in sex-specific neurons, despite early birth, suggests that sexual maturation signals trigger neurotransmitter specification in these neurons.

results.result: The AIM interneuron pair exhibits sexually dimorphic neurotransmitter identity: glutamatergic (eat-4/VGLUT+) in hermaphrodites, but undergoing a neurotransmitter switch in males from glutamatergic (L1-L3) to cholinergic (L4 onwards, with eat-4 downregulation and unc-17/cho-1 induction).
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C103 are supported by expression data in Figure 5D-E showing the temporal dynamics of the neurotransmitter switch. This is a novel finding demonstrating that neurotransmitter identity can be sexually dimorphic and developmentally regulated in the same neuron type.

results.result: The neurotransmitter switch in AIM neurons is programmed cell-autonomously, as demonstrated by masculinization of AIM in hermaphrodites (eat-4prom11::fem-3) causing eat-4 downregulation and cho-1 upregulation, while feminization of AIM in males (tra-2ic expression) maintains eat-4 and prevents cho-1 induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C106 are supported by cell-specific sex-reversal experiments in Figure 5F. The reciprocal effects of masculinization and feminization provide strong evidence for cell-autonomous control of the neurotransmitter switch by the sex determination pathway.

results.result: Previous work identified transcriptional regulators of cholinergic identity: unc-86 (POU homeobox) controls IL2, URA, URB sensory neurons; ttx-3 (LIM homeobox) controls AIY and AIA interneurons; and unc-3 (COE Zn-finger) controls VNC motor neurons and SAB head motor neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C109 summarize prior work from the authors' lab (Zhang et al., 2014; Altun-Gultekin et al., 2001; Kratsios et al., 2011, 2015). These claims provide context for the new regulatory factors identified in this study.

results.result: Seven transcriptional regulators control cholinergic identity of 20 of 52 cholinergic neuron types, with a striking preponderance of homeodomain-containing proteins among the newly identified regulators.
results.evaluation: Claims C110 and C111 are supported by data in Table 6 and Figure 6. The preponderance of homeodomain proteins is consistent with prior observations for glutamatergic identity (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013) and suggests a general principle of neurotransmitter identity specification.

results.result: Three LIM homeobox genes (lim-4, lin-11, ceh-14) control cholinergic identity of six distinct neuron types across sensory, inter-, and motor neurons, but lim-7 (C. elegans Islet homolog) is not required for cholinergic identity despite its role in vertebrate cholinergic specification.
results.evaluation: Claim C112 is supported by data in Table 6 and Figure 6. Claim C113 is supported by the authors' observations (data not shown) and citation to Cho et al., 2014. The finding that different LIM homeobox family members are used in C. elegans vs. vertebrates suggests evolutionary divergence in the specific factors used, despite conservation of the gene family's role.

results.result: Additional homeodomain transcription factors control cholinergic identity: unc-30 (Pitx) controls PVP (with lin-11); unc-86 (POU) controls URX, RIH, and male CEM neurons; unc-86 and ceh-14 together control male AIM cholinergic identity and hermaphrodite/early male AIM glutamatergic identity; all factors are continuously expressed, suggesting roles in both initiation and maintenance.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C118 are supported by expression and mutant analysis data in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The continuous expression pattern (C118) supports the inference that these factors maintain as well as initiate cholinergic identity.

results.result: unc-42 (Prox-type homeobox), identified from an EMS genetic screen, regulates cholinergic identity in RMD motor neurons and four additional cholinergic head neuron types, and is continuously expressed in all regulated neuron types.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121 are supported by genetic screen results and expression/mutant analysis in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The identification of unc-42 through an unbiased genetic screen validates the approach and identifies a new regulator of cholinergic identity.

results.result: unc-3 regulates cholinergic identity genes (cho-1 and unc-17) in all command interneurons (AVA, AVB, AVD, AVE, PVC) and tail neurons (PDA, PDB, PVN, DVA), as confirmed by fosmid reporter and CRISPR-Cas9 gfp knock-in showing unc-3 expression in all these neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C124 are supported by mutant analysis in Figure 7 and Table 6, and expression analysis in Figure 7A. The extension of unc-3 function beyond motor neurons to command interneurons is a major new finding that reveals unc-3's role in circuit-level identity specification.

results.result: Most transcriptional regulators of cholinergic identity also control other identity features: unc-3 affects PDA identity markers (exp-1, ace-3/4, cog-1); unc-42 affects RMD mgl-1 expression; ceh-14 affects AIM neuropeptide (flp-10), serotonergic identity, and PVC glutamate receptors (nmr-1, glr-1); lin-11 and unc-30 control many PVP features; lim-4 controls multiple AWB features.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C130 are supported by mutant analysis data in Figure 8 and citations to prior work (Hutter, 2003; Alqadah et al., 2015; Sagasti et al., 1999). The pleiotropic effects of these transcription factors indicate they are terminal selectors that coordinate multiple aspects of neuronal identity.

results.result: The serotonergic identity of HSN motor neurons is controlled by unc-86, but unc-86 does not affect unc-17/VAChT expression in HSN.
results.evaluation: Claims C131 and C132 are supported by citation to Sze et al., 2002 and the authors' observations (data not shown). This represents an exception to the general pattern of transcription factors controlling multiple identity features, suggesting that cholinergic and serotonergic identities in HSN are independently regulated.

results.result: unc-3 shows differential activity in different neuron types: in motor neurons (SAB, A-, B-, AS-type VNC MNs), unc-3 controls cholinergic identity and many other markers; in command interneurons (AVA, AVB, AVD, AVE, PVC) and DVA, unc-3 activity is restricted to cholinergic identity, with no effect on >10 other identity markers (glutamate receptors, neuropeptides, ion channels), while other transcription factors (unc-42, fax-1, cfi-1) control subsets of these unc-3-independent markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C136 are supported by prior work (Kratsios et al., 2015, 2011) and extensive marker analysis in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Table 7-8. The cell-type-specific activity of unc-3 represents a remarkable departure from the typical pattern of terminal selectors and suggests modular control of neuronal identity features.

results.result: unc-3 is expressed and required for cholinergic identity in all neurons of the ventral nerve cord motor circuit, making it a circuit-associated transcription factor that defines the ability of neurons in the circuit to communicate with each other.
results.evaluation: Claims C137 and C138 are supported by expression and mutant data in Figure 9A and Figure 7B. The pan-circuit expression and function of unc-3 represents a novel organizational principle where a single transcription factor coordinates neurotransmitter identity across an entire functional circuit.

results.result: In unc-3 mutants, UNC-7::GFP puncta (electrical synapses) are severely reduced, but transcriptional unc-7 reporter expression is unaffected, indicating that unc-3 affects electrical synapse formation at a post-transcriptional step independent of innexin expression regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C141 are supported by data in Figure 7C. The differential effect on translational vs. transcriptional reporters provides strong evidence for a post-transcriptional mechanism. However, the specific step affected remains to be determined.

results.result: In unc-3 null mutants, AVA shows connectivity defects at all levels: reduced chemical synaptic input from other command interneurons and reduced output to motor neurons and command interneurons, with overall axonal process disorganization in the VNC, though AVA still neighbors its normal synaptic partners, indicating connectivity defects are not secondary to placement defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C144 are supported by EM reconstruction data in Figure 7D. The detailed connectivity analysis demonstrates that unc-3 is required not only for neurotransmitter identity but also for proper synapse formation within the motor circuit. The observation that AVA remains adjacent to its partners (C144) strengthens the conclusion that connectivity defects are primary.

results.result: Non-cholinergic synaptic inputs from sensory neurons into the motor circuit are not affected by unc-3, as demonstrated by unaffected GRASP signals for the glutamatergic PHB to AVA connection.
results.evaluation: Claims C145 and C146 are supported by GRASP analysis (data not shown) and citations to White et al., 1986 and Park et al., 2011. This control experiment demonstrates specificity of unc-3's effects to cholinergic circuit components.

results.result: Pan-circuit control of cholinergic identity by unc-3 is mediated via a single UNC-3 binding site (COE motif); deletion of this motif in the cho-1 fosmid eliminates expression in all unc-3-dependent neurons, but a 280bp cho-1 or 250bp unc-17 fragment containing the COE motif only drives expression in motor neurons, not interneurons, suggesting unc-3 cooperates with distinct cofactors in different neuron types.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C150 are supported by fosmid reporter and minimal promoter analysis in Figure 10A-E. The requirement for a single COE motif is striking, but the differential activity of minimal promoters (C149) suggests additional regulatory elements are needed for interneuron expression, supporting the cofactor hypothesis (C150).

results.result: unc-3 activity is required for both neurotransmitter identity and synaptic connectivity throughout the VNC motor circuit (motor neurons and command interneurons), but is not required for expression of other command interneuron identity features such as glutamate receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C151 and C152 are supported by the combined data from neurotransmitter marker analysis (Figure 7B), connectivity analysis (Figure 7C-D), and other marker analysis (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). This summary accurately captures the dual role of unc-3 in neurotransmitter specification and circuit assembly, while highlighting its restricted activity in command interneurons.

results.result: unc-42 is frequently employed in 'regulated mutual' 3-neuron network motifs, specifying cholinergic identity of cross-connected head motor neurons (RMDs, SMDs) and the RIV interneuron that innervates them, but in cross-connected command interneurons, unc-42 does not affect cholinergic identity, instead affecting expression of multiple ionotropic glutamate receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C155 are supported by network motif analysis, expression data, and citation to Brockie et al., 2001. The differential activity of unc-42 in different motif contexts parallels the cell-type-specific activity of unc-3 and suggests modular circuit assembly.

results.result: unc-42 controls and coordinates presynaptic neurotransmitter identity and postsynaptic receptor expression in a repulsive reflex circuit: glutamatergic identity of ASH sensory neurons, cholinergic identity of cross-connected head motor neurons coupled by electrical synapses, glutamate receptor expression in command interneurons, and glutamatergic identity of AIB interneurons, forming an interconnected network in the head.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C160 are supported by prior work (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013), current data, and unpublished data (C159). The comprehensive role of unc-42 in coordinating multiple aspects of circuit function across different neurotransmitter systems is well-documented in Figure 9B, though claim C159 relies on unpublished data.
